title: Quantum Approximation Complexity of Classical Optimization Problems
abstract: Classical approximation complexity asks what solution quality can be guaranteed with polynomial-time computation. The classes APX, PTAS, and FPTAS distinguish a fixed approximation ratio, approximation to any fixed accuracy, and approximation schemes whose running time is also polynomial in inverse accuracy. Their randomized counterparts are R-APX, R-PTAS, and R-FPTAS. We define bounded-error quantum counterparts BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, and BQ-FPTAS. Membership requires a uniform quantum algorithm that, on every input, returns a feasible classical solution achieving at least the claimed approximation ratio with probability at least 2/3. Scores (objective values) must be efficiently classically computable. Running time includes parameter selection, preparation, measurement, decoding, and repetition. Many quantum optimization methods are used heuristically, and high benchmark scores alone do not establish these guarantees. We further establish a conditional hierarchy for logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential approximation factors.   Assuming NP $\nsubseteq$ BQP, the quantum classes form a strict hierarchy. Problems based on prime factorization and discrete logarithms give conditional quantum-classical separations. Certified Maximum Order has an exact quantum algorithm, while any randomized polynomial-time algorithm guaranteeing at least an inverse-polynomial approximation ratio on every input would yield efficient factoring. Discrete-Logarithm Fitting has an exact quantum algorithm and a deterministic one-half approximation, but any fixed improvement over one half would give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the safe-prime discrete logarithm problem. Our results show, under explicit complexity assumptions, that quantum computation can improve worst-case approximation guarantees. A quantum-classical gap for common problems such as MaxCut or MaxSAT remains open.
summary:
This paper rigorously defines quantum complexity classes for approximating solutions to classical optimization problems. It establishes a strict hierarchy among these quantum classes, demonstrating that quantum computation can yield provable worst-case improvements over classical algorithms for certain problems, provided that $	ext{NP}

main_problem: The paper investigates the quantum approximation complexity of classical optimization problems, aiming to determine the best solution quality achievable using quantum computation compared to classical methods.
main_result: Under the assumption that NP is not contained in BQP, the quantum complexity classes form a strict hierarchy (BQ-FPTAS $\subsetneq$ BQ-PTAS $\subsetneq$ BQ-APX), and quantum computation can provide worst-case improvements over classical guarantees for certain problems.
method: The authors define quantum counterparts to classical approximation classes (BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, BQ-FPTAS) and use conditional separations based on the hardness of problems like factoring and discrete logarithms to establish these theoretical gaps.
model_or_system: The analysis is purely theoretical, focusing on computational complexity classes (APX, PTAS, etc.) and the computational power of quantum algorithms (BQP) applied to classical optimization problems.
key_observables: Approximation ratios ($\alpha, ho$), success probability (fixed at $\ge 2/3$), and the relationship between the expected score and the guaranteed output ratio.
important_parameters:
The complexity assumptions, notably $	ext{NP} 
ot\subseteq 	ext{BQP}$, and the specific approximation factors (e.g., one-half for DLog-Fit).
main_assumptions:
The entire framework relies on the assumption that $	ext{NP} 
ot\subseteq 	ext{BQP}$, and the analysis for specific problems assumes the hardness of factoring or discrete logarithms.

paper_structure: The paper first defines the quantum approximation complexity classes, then establishes the hierarchy relationships, and finally proves conditional separations using specific number-theoretic problems (like factoring and discrete logarithms) to demonstrate quantum advantages.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO physics, the rigorous framework for quantifying computational advantage (quantum vs. classical) is foundational for understanding the limits of quantum simulation and computation in physical systems.
